notes.meaning: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit. In Hebrew, the word for 'summer fruit' sounds almost like the word for 'end'. The picture is that Israel's sin is fully ripe and God's long patience is over. Like fruit that must be eaten at once, judgment will come soon, and God will no longer 'pass by' or overlook their sins.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The old Latin Bible used by the Catholic Church reads the basket as a hook for pulling down fruit. Jerome explained it as God drawing the time of captivity closer.

notes.meaning: On that day, happy songs will turn into loud cries of grief. There will be so many dead bodies that they are thrown out without proper funerals. The silence may come from fear of the enemy, from too many dead to mourn, or from people being told to bow quietly under God's hand.

Amos speaks to the rich and powerful who 'pant after' the poor like hungry animals. They keep the holy days on the outside but can't wait for them to end so they can get back to business. They cheat three ways: smaller measures of grain, heavier weights for the buyer's money, and rigged scales. They even sell sweepings from the floor as grain, and push the poor into slavery over debts as small as a pair of sandals.

God makes a solemn promise, swearing by 'the Pride of Jacob'. Many take this to mean God himself, the one Israel should glory in. Others take it as the special privileges he gave Israel. 'I will never forget' means he will not let these wrongs go unpunished.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The old Latin Bible reads it as God swearing against Jacob's pride, so the phrase points to Israel's arrogance.

notes.meaning: Such wrongs will make the land shake, and everyone in it will mourn. The whole land will heave up and sink back down, like the Nile River in Egypt when it floods. Many see an earthquake here. Others see a flood of trouble that sweeps the people away.

God will make the sun go down at noon. Disaster will strike suddenly, right in the middle of Israel's good times, when people feel safest. Darkness at midday is a picture of great trouble coming without warning.

differ.view: It is a figure of speech for sudden punishment on people lulled by wealth, not a literal eclipse.
Wesley saw Israel's sun setting at noon in the plots and civil wars before Assyria invaded. Clarke allowed for real darkness from an earthquake or eclipse.
Some see a prophecy of the darkness at noon on the day Jesus died on the cross.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Many early church fathers, honored in both churches, linked this verse to the darkness at Christ's crucifixion.

notes.meaning: Their happy feasts and songs will turn to weeping. People wore rough sackcloth and shaved their heads to show grief, and everyone will do so. The sorrow will be like parents losing their only son, the deepest grief there is. Worse, things will not get better; the end will be a bitter day.

God warns of a famine worse than hunger for bread or thirst for water: a famine of hearing his word. The people refused to listen to his prophets, so the prophets would fall silent. Commentators call this one of the heaviest judgments, because God's word feeds the soul.

differ.view: Some stress that the famine lies mainly in the hearers, who have grown unable to hear, rather than in God holding back his word.

notes.meaning: People will stagger across the whole land, from sea to sea and from north to east, looking for a message from God, but they will not find one. Some note that the south is left out. That was where Jerusalem and the true worship were, and they still would not go there. Their searching comes from pain and fear, not from a real wish to obey God.

Even the strongest and most beautiful young men and women will faint from thirst. If the young and strong give way, the weak will fare even worse. The thirst is for God's word, and also for every good thing they will lack.

Those who make their promises in the name of idols will fall and never get up again. 'The guilt of Samaria' means the golden calf idol at Bethel. 'Your god, O Dan' is the other golden calf, in the far north. 'The way of Beersheba' means the kind of worship done there. They gave idols the honor that belongs only to God.
